payload.prompt: Four real U.S. companies, anonymized, most recent fiscal year (10-K data). Two report no gross-profit line at all, and two report gross margins above 70% — the remaining lines must split each pair. Match each to its industry.

stats.name: Gross margin
stats.value: not reported — one block of 'total costs and deductions'

tells.A: No gross-profit line plus two-thirds of assets in productive plant says extraction-and-processing at commodity scale. The tie-break against Company D (the other no-gross-margin filer): an 8.7% net margin at 0.74x asset turnover means it sells a lot of something it cannot price — a commodity — while D's 29% margin means priced infrastructure. Heavy D&A (7.8% of revenue) matched by even heavier capex is the perpetual drilling treadmill of an integrated oil major.
tells.B: A 74% gross margin eaten down to a 12% net margin is the pharmaceutical signature: the pill is nearly free to make, but R&D (16.7% of revenue) and selling costs consume the spread. Confirmation is on the balance sheet and in the clocks — 60% of assets are goodwill and acquired intangibles (pipelines bought, not built) and inventory sits some 240 days because drugs take most of a year to manufacture and release.
tells.C: The other 70%+ gross margin — but with a 55.6% NET margin, which no pharma or software-services company prints. PP&E at just 5% of assets is the tell that the physical product is manufactured by someone else: a fabless semiconductor designer keeping the design margin while foundries hold the factories. Slow inventory (125 days of prepaid wafer pipeline) on a hardware seller confirms it.
tells.D: No COGS, essentially no inventory, and 86% of assets in plant is a network business that sells the use of infrastructure, not goods. Operating margin of 40% at a glacial 0.35x asset turnover is the freight railroad trade: irreplaceable track converts capital intensity into pricing power. Compare A: same missing gross-profit line, opposite margin story.

hints.text: Pair them first: two have no gross margin (asset-heavy sellers of commodity or capacity), two are above 70% (sellers of ideas). Then let net margin split each pair.
PP&E as a share of assets runs 5% → 67% → 86% across three of these. Who outsources the factory, who owns the wells, who owns the track?

explanation: A is Exxon Mobil (FY2025), B is Pfizer (FY2025), C is NVIDIA (FY2026), D is Union Pacific (FY2025). The drill is deliberate pairing: the two no-gross-margin filers split on net margin (8.7% commodity price-taker vs 29.1% network owner), and the two 70%+ gross margins split on what happens below the gross line (pharma's margin is consumed by R&D and SG&A; the fabless designer keeps 56 cents of every dollar). Margins sort industries only when you read them at both altitudes.

payload.prompt: Four real consumer-facing U.S. companies, anonymized, most recent fiscal year (10-K data). All four sell directly to households — the statements must tell you HOW. Match each to its business.

stats.name: Largest single asset
stats.value: capitalized self-produced content, 59% of total assets

stats.name: Effective tax rate
stats.value: NEGATIVE ≈18% — a net tax benefit on positive pretax income

stats.name: Total equity
stats.value: NEGATIVE $8.1B (retained earnings itself is a deficit)

stats.name: Operating lease right-of-use assets / total assets
Net margin
stats.value: 5.0%, after operating margin halved in one year

stats.name: Dividends paid
stats.value: $2.8B — more than the year's net income

tells.A: The most extreme velocity machine in the roster: 12.8% gross margin (half a grocer's) survivable only at 3.6x asset turnover, with 28-day inventory collected in 4 days. The killer detail is payables exceeding inventory — the membership warehouse retailer sells goods before paying for them, and the real profit is the membership fee collected up front.
tells.B: No inventory, no receivables, almost no plant — but 59% of assets is a library of self-produced shows, capitalized when made and amortized when watched. Rising operating margin (20.6% → 29.5%) on a subscription top line is streaming's operating leverage: content costs are fixed, members are not.
tells.C: 73% of assets in plant turning over 0.13x, with a fat regulated margin, is a utility before any other clue. The renewables developer inside it shows in two lines no ordinary utility prints: a persistently NEGATIVE effective tax rate (credits for building wind and solar) and noncontrolling interests at 18% of equity (project slices sold to tax-equity partners).
tells.D: Negative equity from decades of buybacks, a balance sheet 29% capitalized store leases, and customer stored-value float in deferred revenue: a chain that operates thousands of rented coffeehouses. The current-year distress markers — operating margin halved, dividends exceeding net income, buybacks stopped — date it to the turnaround year.

hints.text: Asset turnover spans 0.13x to 3.6x across these four. Rank them first — velocity is the fastest sorter of consumer business models.
One has negative equity and one has $93B of happily rising debt. Neither is in trouble — explain why for each and you have identified both.

explanation: A is Costco (FY2025), B is Netflix (FY2025), C is NextEra Energy (FY2025), D is Starbucks (FY2025). Four ways to sell to a household: at cost with a membership fee (velocity, supplier-financed inventory), by subscription to a capitalized content library (operating leverage), through a regulated meter (capital intensity with guaranteed margins and subsidized taxes), and over a rented counter (leases everywhere, equity hollowed out by buybacks). Same customer, four unmistakable silhouettes.

payload.prompt: Compute NVIDIA's gross margin for fiscal 2026 (year ended January 25, 2026), as a percentage of revenue.
payload.context:
NVIDIA, fiscal 2026 10-K ($M):
Revenue: 215,938
Cost of revenue: 62,475
For reference, gross margin was 72.7% in fiscal 2024 and 75.0% in fiscal 2025.

hints.text: Gross profit = revenue − cost of revenue; divide by revenue. Then compare it to the two prior years given in the context.

explanation: (215,938 − 62,475) / 215,938 = 71.1%. Two lessons in one number. First the level: 71 cents of gross profit per hardware dollar exists only because NVIDIA is fabless — the foundry owns the factory, NVIDIA owns the design. Second the trajectory: 72.7% → 75.0% → 71.1%. Margin fell almost four points in the newest year even as revenue grew 65%, which is the question an analyst must chase: mix shift toward lower-margin systems, pricing given to win the biggest customers, or ramp costs on a new architecture? A falling margin on exploding revenue is not distress — but it is the first place competition would show up, so it earns a note every single quarter.

payload.prompt: Starbucks' total equity is NEGATIVE $8.1B, so return on equity and debt-to-equity are meaningless — the denominator is upside down. Lenders reach for coverage instead. Compute Starbucks' interest coverage (operating income / interest expense) for fiscal 2025 (year ended September 28, 2025).
payload.context:
Starbucks, fiscal 2025 10-K ($M):
Operating income: 2,936.6
Interest expense: 542.6
For reference: fiscal 2023 operating income was 5,870.8 on interest expense of 550.1.

hints.text: Coverage = operating income / interest expense: how many times this year's operating profit could pay the interest bill.
When equity is negative, every equity-denominator ratio (ROE, D/E) produces a nonsense sign. Solvency analysis shifts to flow measures: coverage, and debt against EBITDA or cash flow.

explanation: 2,936.6 / 542.6 = 5.4x. The framing is the real lesson: with equity at −$8.1B, ROE would be a negative number on a profitable company and debt-to-equity would be negative too — arithmetic garbage. Negative book equity (here from decades of buybacks, not losses) forces the analyst to flow-based solvency measures, and those tell a real story: coverage was 10.7x in fiscal 2023 (5,870.8/550.1) and has halved to 5.4x, entirely from the numerator — operating profit fell by half in the turnaround year while the interest bill stayed flat. Still investment-grade comfortable, but the direction is the warning. One more layer for the careful: $10.5B of operating lease liabilities are fixed store-rent obligations that behave like debt, so lease-adjusted coverage is materially tighter than this headline.
